729.title: Abu Bakr, as-Siddiq
729.hook: Abu Bakr believes without hesitation and brings others: Uthman, Talhah, Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman, Sa'd
729.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims know Abu Bakr as as-Siddiq, say 'may Allah be pleased with him' after his name, and honor him as the first caliph; Shia Muslims read the succession after the Prophet differently. His early belief is retold in sirah study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first to believe: Khadijah, Ali, Zayd, Abu Bakr. Who did you thank for believing in you first? Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

Some answers take weeks. Others come before the question is finished. In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is remembered as saying that everyone he invited to Islam hesitated, held back, thought it over, except one man. When he told Abu Bakr, Abu Bakr did not hold back and did not hesitate. A merchant of Quraysh, well known and well liked, a man people came to with their business and their questions. He hears it, and he says yes. Today: Abu Bakr.

His title is as-Siddiq. Tradition explains it through sidq, truthfulness: a siddiq is someone who confirms the truth, who takes a true word as true. There's a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from a later quarrel among the companions, where the Prophet defends him with a memory: when he was sent, people said, you are lying, and Abu Bakr said, he has spoken the truth, and stood by him with himself and his wealth. That is what the name holds. Sirah writers also tell that the title stuck after the Night Journey, when Abu Bakr was told the Prophet claimed to have gone to Jerusalem and back in a night, and answered that if he said it, it was true. That story belongs later in the year; here it shows how the name was understood. Now the second half of the day. Abu Bakr didn't keep his yes to himself. Ibn Ishaq names the men who came to Islam through him: Uthman ibn Affan, az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and Talhah ibn Ubaydullah. Names that will come back again and again in the story. He brought them to the Prophet, and they believed. How? Ibn Ishaq describes him as a man people liked to sit with, who knew the genealogies of Quraysh, who was easy and kind in company. His friends trusted him, so they listened. The same quality that made him believe at once made others willing to hear.
screen: `AS-SIDDIQ: WHO CONFIRMS THE TRUTH.` · `HE HAS SPOKEN THE TRUTH.` · `HE BRINGS HIS FRIENDS.` · `TRUSTED, SO THEY LISTENED.` · then, large: `HE BELIEVED AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: The practice: bring a friend to something good. Settle in, breathe slowly. Think of one good thing in your life that has helped you: a class, a walk, a habit, a place of worship, a book, a kind group of people. Then think of one friend who might be glad of it. Not someone you need to convince. Someone who trusts you. See yourself telling them, simply, without pressure. If you pray, you can ask for that friend's good. Rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Abu Bakr. The friend who said yes without hesitating, called as-Siddiq, the one who confirms the truth, and who brought others with him. Today's word.
Your line: he believed at once. Today, invite one friend to one good thing, and let your yes be quick when it's a good one. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

730.title: The house of al-Arqam
730.hook: early Muslims meet in secret at a young man's house to learn and pray
730.howItsDone: Muslims remember Dar al-Arqam in sirah study as the house where the early believers met to learn and pray; Muslims still gather in small study circles to learn the Qur'an together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr, as-Siddiq. Your line was: he believed at once. Did you bring a friend to something good? Day seven hundred thirty.

A door near the hill of Safa, in the middle of Mecca. People come to it one at a time, not in a crowd. A merchant. A freed slave. A young man from a powerful clan. Inside, someone is reciting new verses, slowly, so they can be learned by heart. Others are bowing in prayer. Outside, the city goes about its business, and the door stays shut. Today: the house of al-Arqam.
screen: `A DOOR NEAR SAFA.` → `ONE AT A TIME.` → `VERSES LEARNED BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam was one of the early believers, from the clan of Makhzum, and the sirah writers describe him as young when he came to Islam. He had a house near Safa, and he opened it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, used it as a meeting place for the believers, a place to teach, to recite what had come down, and to pray together out of sight. Why out of sight? The sirah tells that the early Muslims at first went out to the valleys around Mecca to pray, and that at least once they were found there and mocked, and it came to blows. A house was safer. So for a stretch of time, this small house became something like a hidden school. Look at who could sit together there. Outside, in Mecca, a person's clan decided much of how they were treated. Inside al-Arqam's house, a freed man and a merchant of Quraysh could sit in the same room and learn the same verses from the same teacher. Sirah writers later called it Dar al-Arqam, the house of al-Arqam, and some of them tell of people who came to Islam within its walls. Notice too what made it possible: one young man saying, use my house. He didn't preach in the street. He offered a room near Safa, with a door that could be shut.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN OPENS HIS HOUSE.` · `FROM THE VALLEYS TO A ROOM.` · `A FREED MAN BESIDE A MERCHANT.` · `HE OFFERED A ROOM.` · then, large: `DAR AL-ARQAM.`

segments.voice: The practice: find a quiet place and be there for two minutes. A closed room, a parked car, a corner of a stairwell, a bench under a tree. If you can move, move there now. Sit, and let the noise of the day stay on the other side of the door. If you pray, you can pray here, simply, the way you know how. If you don't, just breathe, and notice how a small, quiet space changes what you can hear. The bell holds the time.
The house of al-Arqam. A young believer's house near Safa, where the early Muslims met to learn and to pray out of sight. Today's word.
Your line: a hidden school. Today, find one quiet room, even for a minute, and learn or pray one small thing there. Day seven hundred thirty.

731.title: Three years quietly
731.hook: for about three years the call is private, person to person
731.howItsDone: In sirah study Muslims divide the Meccan call into a private stage and a public stage, and the early private stage is often discussed as a model of patient, personal invitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the house of al-Arqam. Your line was: a hidden school. Did you find a quiet room, even for a minute? Day seven hundred thirty-one.

No speeches. No crowd gathered at the hill. For a long stretch at the beginning, the message in Mecca travels the way a secret recipe travels in a family: one person leans toward another and says, come, let me tell you something. A friend to a friend. A brother to a sister. A master's household to a servant. Ibn Ishaq, the early biographer, gives this quiet season a length. Today: three years quietly.
screen: `NO SPEECHES. NO CROWDS.` → `ONE PERSON TO ANOTHER.` → `A QUIET SEASON.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq writes that three years passed between the time the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, kept his message private and the time he was commanded to make it public. Some other writers count the time differently, so hold the number loosely; the shape is what the sirah keeps. First quietly, then openly. What did quiet look like? It looked like the last few days of this path. Khadijah in the house. Ali and Zayd at the table. Abu Bakr bringing his friends, one conversation at a time. Prayer in the valleys, then behind al-Arqam's door. People who heard it heard it from someone they already knew, face to face, with time for questions. Why begin that way? The sources don't give one reason, and readers offer several. Some point to protection: a small group was easy to crush. Some point to teaching: the first believers needed time to learn the verses and pray together before anything was asked of them in public. Some simply notice that this is how trust moves, from someone you know. Then the season ends. The Qur'an gives a command that Pickthall translates: "So proclaim that which thou art commanded." And another verse tells him to warn his nearest kin. What he does with that command is tomorrow's story. Today is the quiet before it, and the quiet was not empty. It built the people who would stand beside him.
screen: `FIRST QUIETLY, THEN OPENLY.` · `FACE TO FACE, ONE AT A TIME.` · `PROTECTION, TEACHING, TRUST.` · `THE COMMAND TO PROCLAIM.` · then, large: `SO PROCLAIM THAT WHICH THOU ART COMMANDED.`

segments.voice: The practice: share one good thing privately. Breathe, and settle. Start with the other side of it. Recall a time someone told you something good one to one, not in front of a room: a piece of advice, a line of scripture, a word of praise. How was it said? Where were you sitting? What made it easy to hear? Keep that manner. Then choose one small good thing of your own to pass on, to one person, the same way: no audience, no post, just the two of you. If you pray, you can ask that it reach them well. The bell holds the time.
Three years quietly. The private season of the call, person to person, before the command came to proclaim it. Ibn Ishaq gives the length. Today's word.
Your line: quietly first. Today, tell one good thing to one person, privately, and let it go no further than that. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

732.title: The call from Safa
732.hook: he climbs Safa and asks, would you believe me if I said an army was behind this hill
732.howItsDone: Muslims retell the call from Safa as the beginning of the public message in Mecca; pilgrims on Hajj and Umrah walk between Safa and Marwah, though that rite remembers Hajar, not this day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three years quietly. Your line was: quietly first. Who did you tell one good thing to, just between the two of you? Day seven hundred thirty-two.

Ya sabahah! The cry goes up from the little hill of Safa. It's the alarm call, the one people shout when raiders are coming at dawn. Men drop what they're doing and come running. Those who can't come send someone to find out what's happening. The clans of Quraysh gather at the foot of the hill and look up. Standing on top is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The quiet season is over. Today: the call from Safa.
screen: `A CRY FROM THE HILL.` → `THE CLANS COME RUNNING.` → `THE QUIET SEASON IS OVER.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene from Ibn Abbas. When the verse came, warn thy nearest kin, he climbed Safa and called the clans by name. When they had gathered, he did not begin with a sermon. He began with a question. If I told you that horsemen in the valley were about to attack you, would you believe me? And they answered, yes, we have only ever known you to tell the truth. Then he said: I am a warner to you, before a severe punishment. Look at how he builds it. He lets the city testify to his honesty before he says a single new thing. Years of trust, from the market, from the black stone, from Khadijah's caravans, are called in with one question. And the word he uses for himself is nadhir, a warner. Not a ruler, not a fortune-teller. Someone who has seen what's coming and shouts so others can get ready, the way the alarm call itself works. It is a word the Qur'an also uses for him. The report also says that one voice in the crowd answered him with a curse. Who it was, and what came back, is tomorrow. Today hold the question. Would you believe me? It asks what kind of life makes a person believable when it matters.
screen: `HE CALLS THE CLANS BY NAME.` · `WOULD YOU BELIEVE ME?` · `YOU HAVE ONLY TOLD THE TRUTH.` · `NADHIR: A WARNER.` · then, large: `WOULD YOU BELIEVE ME?`

segments.voice: The practice: speak one truth plainly. Settle and breathe. Think of one true thing you've been softening, avoiding or wrapping in extra words: a no, an apology, a concern, a thank-you. Find the plainest way to say it. One sentence, no decorations. Say it silently to yourself until it sounds clean. If it's safe and kind to say out loud today, plan when. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to say it well. The bell holds the time.
The call from Safa. The Prophet climbs the hill, asks the clans if they'd believe him, and names himself a warner. Today's word.
Your line: would you believe me? Today, say one true thing plainly, the kind of plain that keeps you believable. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

733.title: The uncle who cursed
733.hook: Abu Lahab curses him in front of all, and Surah al-Masad answers
733.tomorrow: The sun in my right hand
733.howItsDone: Surah al-Masad (111) is a short surah that Muslims memorize and can recite in prayer; its occasion, Abu Lahab's words at Safa, is taught alongside it in tafsir and sirah study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the call from Safa. Your line was: would you believe me? What true thing did you say plainly? Day seven hundred thirty-three.

Back to the foot of Safa. The clans have just said, we have only known you to tell the truth. He has just called himself a warner, before a severe punishment. Some of them had left their work to come. Then a voice cuts across the crowd. Not a stranger's voice. His own uncle's. Al-Bukhari keeps the words in Ibn Abbas's report: may you perish, was it for this that you gathered us? Today: the uncle who cursed.
screen: `THE CROWD AT SAFA.` → `A VOICE CUTS ACROSS IT.` → `HIS OWN UNCLE.`

segments.voice: He's known as Abu Lahab. That's a kunya, a 'father of' name, and tradition reads it as father of flame; the sources give his given name as Abd al-Uzza. He was a son of Abd al-Muttalib, a brother of the Prophet's father, and he lived close by. Family. That is what makes the moment sting. The report in al-Bukhari says that after his words, a surah came down: surah one hundred eleven, al-Masad, the palm fiber. Pickthall translates its first verse: "The power of Abu Lahab will perish, and he will perish." The surah goes on to say his wealth will not help him, and it speaks of his wife carrying firewood, with a rope of palm fiber around her neck, which gives the surah its name. The tradition reads it as Allah's answer, not as a nephew trading insults with his uncle. And look at what is missing from the scene. On Safa, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is not reported to curse back. In the tradition's reading, the reply is the surah. There's a small hadith in al-Bukhari that shows the same habit later. Quraysh took to calling him Mudhammam, the blamed one, a twist on Muhammad, the praised one. He said to his companions: doesn't it amaze you how Allah turns their insults away from me? They curse Mudhammam, and I am Muhammad. The insult missed. That's the shape of today. A curse came at him in public, from family. He didn't answer it with another. As the tradition tells it, the answer belonged to Allah, and the insult fell on a name that wasn't his.
screen: `ABU LAHAB, HIS UNCLE.` · `SURAH AL-MASAD ANSWERS.` · `HE DOES NOT CURSE BACK.` · `THEY CURSE MUDHAMMAM.` · then, large: `THE POWER OF ABU LAHAB WILL PERISH.`

segments.voice: The practice: don't answer a curse with one. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind one sharp word someone threw at you, recently or long ago, maybe from family. If it still sits somewhere in your body, a jaw or a chest, just notice where. You don't have to forgive it right now, or pretend it didn't hurt. Just practice not throwing one back, even in your head. Each time a reply rises, breathe out, and let it drop. If you pray, you can leave the matter with Allah. The bell holds the time.
The uncle who cursed. Abu Lahab, who answered the call from Safa with a curse, and the surah al-Masad that came in reply. Today's word.
Your line: let it go. Today, when a sharp word comes your way, let it miss: don't send one back. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

734.title: The sun in my right hand
734.word: The sun in my right hand
734.hook: the sirah tells of his answer to Quraysh's offers: even if they put the sun in one hand and the moon in the other, he would not stop
734.howItsDone: Muslims retell the sun-and-moon answer in sermons and sirah classes as a picture of steadfastness under pressure; scholars of hadith discuss how strongly the report is transmitted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the uncle who cursed. Your line was: let it go. Did a sharp word come your way, and did you let it miss? Day seven hundred thirty-four.

What would it take? That's the question the leaders of Quraysh start asking once the message is public. The sirah says they try offers. Money, if he wants money. Honor, if he wants honor. Leadership, a crown even, if that's what he's after. And if it's some sickness, they'll pay for a healer. It's a generous list. They also try pressure, on the man who protects him: his uncle. Today: the sun in my right hand.
screen: `WHAT WOULD IT TAKE?` → `MONEY, HONOR, A CROWN.` → `PRESSURE ON HIS UNCLE.`

segments.voice: This story comes to us through the sirah, from Ibn Ishaq. The elders of Quraysh go to Abu Talib and press him: stop your nephew, or step aside and let us deal with him. Abu Talib is shaken. He calls the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and in effect says, spare me, and spare yourself; don't put on me more than I can carry. And the nephew answers with the line that names today. As Ibn Ishaq tells it: O my uncle, by Allah, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left, on condition that I give this up, I would not give it up until Allah makes it prevail or I die in the attempt. Then, Ibn Ishaq says, he wept, and got up to leave. Stay with the picture for a moment. Not gold, not a kingdom: the sun and the moon, placed in two open hands. And still, no. The offer isn't refused because it's too small. It's refused because the thing he carries isn't for sale at any size. The sirah keeps another version of the offers too, where a Qurayshi leader named Utbah comes himself with the list, and the Prophet answers by reciting from the Qur'an, from the surah later called Fussilat, until Utbah goes back to his people looking changed. Two scenes, one answer. And notice the tears. This is not a hard man enjoying a refusal. It costs him to say no to his uncle. What Abu Talib says next is tomorrow.
screen: `QURAYSH PRESS ABU TALIB.` · `SPARE ME, AND SPARE YOURSELF.` · `NOT FOR SALE AT ANY SIZE.` · `UTBAH'S OFFER, AND RECITATION.` · then, large: `THE SUN IN MY RIGHT HAND.`

segments.voice: The practice: refuse one bribe to your values. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself: what's offered to me, small or large, to let go of something I care about? A shortcut at work. A little gossip to fit in. Comfort in place of honesty. Name it. Then hold your hands open on your lap, palms up, as if something shining were placed in them. Feel the weight of the offer, and then quietly turn your palms down. If you pray, you can ask Allah for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
The sun in my right hand. The answer the sirah gives him when Quraysh pressed him through his uncle: not even the sun and the moon. Today's word.
screen: `THE SUN IN MY RIGHT HAND — today's word`.

735.title: Abu Talib's shield
735.hook: his uncle never accepts Islam, yet protects him to the end
735.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Talib's protection of the Prophet in sirah study; Sunni and Shia Muslims differ on his faith, and both speak of his loyalty with honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sun in my right hand. Your line was: the sun in my hand. What small offer did you turn your palm down on? Day seven hundred thirty-five.

We left a nephew in tears, getting up to leave his uncle's house. He has just refused the sun and the moon. His uncle has just asked him to spare them both. Now Abu Talib calls him back. He has every reason to step aside: the leaders of his own tribe are angry with him. Ibn Ishaq gives his words: go, son of my brother, and say what you like; by Allah, I will never hand you over. Today: Abu Talib's shield.
screen: `THE NEPHEW, IN TEARS.` → `THE UNCLE CALLS HIM BACK.` → `I WILL NEVER HAND YOU OVER.`

segments.voice: Abu Talib had taken the boy in after his grandfather died, and raised him with his own children, Ali among them. As the sirah tells it, Abu Talib stood at the head of the Banu Hashim, and while he stood behind his nephew, Quraysh could not simply take him. Quraysh tried to get around it. The sirah tells of a strange offer: they brought him a handsome young man of their own, Umarah ibn al-Walid, and said, take him as your son, and hand us your nephew. Abu Talib's answer, in Ibn Ishaq: you give me your son to feed, and I give you mine to kill? He refused. Then comes the question of his own faith. In Sunni sources, including al-Bukhari, Abu Talib is reported to have died without accepting Islam. Shia tradition holds that he was a believer who kept it hidden to protect his nephew. The two readings differ, and both remember him with honor for what he did. Either way, the outward story is the same: a man who did not publicly follow the message stood between it and harm, at a cost to his standing among his own people. This week has been about people around the Prophet: Abu Bakr believing at once, al-Arqam opening his house, the quiet season, Safa, the uncle who cursed. Two uncles, two sons of Abd al-Muttalib. One cursed him in front of the clans. The other said: I will never hand you over.

segments.voice: The practice: thank someone who protected you without agreeing with you. Settle and breathe. Think of a person who stood up for you, or made room for you, even though they didn't share your choices: a parent with a different faith, a boss who disagreed but backed you, a friend who said, I don't get it, but I'm with you. Ask what it cost them: an argument, some standing, a worry they kept to themselves. Name that cost, quietly. A thank-you that names the cost lands differently. If they're living, plan one way to say it to them. If you pray, you can ask good for them. The bell holds the time.
